# Avascular necrosis

*Categories: Clinical knowledge > Surgery > Trauma and orthopedic surgery > General orthopedics > Avascular necrosis*

[Original Article Link](/library/gF0Fh3)

---

## Summary

Avascular <u>necrosis</u> is a condition in which <u>bone tissue</u> becomes <u>ischemic</u> and begins to suffer pathologic <u>decomposition</u>, leading to <u>joint</u> dysfunction. Avascular <u>necrosis</u> (<u>AVN</u>) affects all age groups and is caused by direct trauma, medications, cellular insult, or mechanical compression, often in the context of predisposing conditions. Susceptible <u>joints</u> include the hip, knee, shoulder, wrist, and ankle. Disease type is typically characterized by location, often with eponymous names. <u>Joint</u> movement is decreased and <u>pain</u> is localized to the affected <u>joint</u>. Patients may be asymptomatic in early stages. <u>X-ray</u> is used for initial imaging, and <u>MRI</u> is required for definitive diagnosis. Management is typically surgical and may include <u>total joint replacement</u> in later stages.




For management specific to avascular <u>necrosis</u> of the hip, see “<u>Osteonecrosis of the femoral head</u>.”

---

## Overview

### Affected structures [[2]](/library/O1WIS40)[[3]](/library/AN1Rdh0)[[4]](/library/Mz1Mtj0)




The <u>bone tissue</u> <u>ischemia</u> and <u>necrosis</u> characteristic of <u>AVN</u> most commonly affect the <u>epiphysis</u> of <u>long bones</u>.




* Hip: femoral head (most common); see also “<u>Osteonecrosis of the femoral head</u>.”

* Knee: <u>medial</u> femoral condyle

* Ankle: talar neck

* Shoulder: <u>humeral head</u>

* Wrist: <u>scaphoid</u>, lunate, <u>capitate</u>

| <u>Legg-Calvé-Perthes disease</u> | <br>* Femoral head<br><br> | <br><br>* Age of onset: 4–10 years<br><br>* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u><br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Idiopathic</u> disease<br><br>* Mismatch between the rapid growth of the femoral <u>epiphyses</u> and the slower development of adequate blood supply to the area<br><br><br> | <br><br>* <u>Antalgic gait</u> (on <u>weight-bearing</u> leg)<br><br>* <u>Pain</u> in the hip or the upper leg, sometimes projecting to the knee<br><br>* Restricted <u>range of movement</u><br><br>* <u>Contralateral</u> involvement in ∼ 10% of cases<br><br><br> |
| Kohler disease | <br>* Tarsal <u>navicular</u><br><br> | <br><br>* Age of onset: 5–10 years<br><br>* <u>♂</u> > <u>♀</u><br><br><br> | <br>* <u>Idiopathic</u> disease<br><br> | <br><br>* Midfoot <u>pain</u><br><br>* Tenderness over the tarsal <u>navicular</u><br><br><br> |
| <br>Freiberg disease <br> | <br>* <u>Metatarsal</u> head (most often II, but also III–V)<br><br> | <br><br>* Age of onset: 10–18 years<br><br>* <u>♀</u> > <u>♂</u><br><br><br> | <br>* More common in children with a long <u>metatarsal</u> II<br><br> | <br>* <u>Pain</u> in the forefoot<br><br> |

## Etiology

* Trauma (e.g., <u>proximal</u> <u>scaphoid fractures</u>)

* Cellular toxicity (e.g., <u>chemotherapy</u>, <u>radiotherapy</u>, <u>thermal injury</u>, smoking, <u>alcohol</u>)

* Medication (e.g., <u>corticosteroids</u>)

* Congenital disease (e.g., <u>sickle cell disease</u>, <u>Gaucher disease</u>)

* Orthopedic conditions (e.g., <u>slipped capital femoral epiphysis</u>, <u>developmental dysplasia of the hip</u>)

* Intraosseous compression (e.g., hemorrhage, elevated <u>bone marrow</u> pressure)

---

## Diagnosis

* Clinical evaluation: history of trauma, <u>glucocorticoid</u> use, or other <u>risk factors for AVN</u>

* <u>X-ray</u>  [[2]](/library/O1WIS40)[[6]](/library/t_1XJj0)[[8]](/library/F_1gJj0)

* First line to rule out acute <u>fracture</u>; may be nondiagnostic in early stages

* Findings include subchondral <u>fracture</u>, <u>sclerosis</u>, cystic changes, and bone collapse.

* <u>MRI</u> without contrast  [[6]](/library/t_1XJj0)[[8]](/library/F_1gJj0)

* <u>Gold standard</u> (highly sensitive) [[2]](/library/O1WIS40)

* Findings depend on the stage and the bone affected.





> [!TIP]
> <u>Glucocorticoid</u> use and chronic <u>heavy drinking</u> are the most common causes of nontraumatic avascular <u>necrosis</u>. [[5]](/library/Lz1wtj0)

## Treatment

Treatment varies depending on location and stage of disease; refer to orthopedics for management as <u>surgery</u> is often required for definitive treatment. See also “<u>Treatment of AVN of the femoral head</u>.” [[5]](/library/Lz1wtj0)




* Treatment goals [[5]](/library/Lz1wtj0)[[6]](/library/t_1XJj0)

* Preventing bone collapse, long-term disability, and <u>chronic pain</u>

* Preserving <u>joint</u> function

* Nonoperative management: for early stages and/or symptomatic relief [[5]](/library/Lz1wtj0)

* Reduce <u>weight-bearing</u> on the <u>joint</u>.

* <u>Pain management</u>

* <u>Risk factor</u> reduction, e.g. <u>smoking cessation</u>

* <u>Physiotherapy</u>

* Surgical treatment

* Core decompression

* Operative decompression of the affected bone to restore <u>perfusion</u>

* May be indicated in early stages [[9]](/library/8z1Ouj0)

* Bone graft

* <u>Joint</u> replacement (e.g., hip, shoulder, knee)





> [!TIP]
> Early detection and prompt treatment significantly improve prognosis. [[5]](/library/Lz1wtj0)
